analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000 and pushes claims into mandatory arbitration.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap malpractice pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000 and force claims into arbitration was introduced by four Senate Republicans in October 1992 and died in the Judiciary Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Sponsored by four Republican senators in the final weeks of 1992, this bill would have required every state to cap malpractice pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000, make each defendant pay only its own share of fault, and cut a patient's award by the amount already paid by health or disability insurance — or lose broad federal funding. It would have pushed malpractice claims arising from Medicare, Medicaid, or employer health plans into nonbinding arbitration, with a claimant who rejected the award and did worse in court forced to pay the provider's legal costs, and it would have applied the same caps to lawsuits against the federal government. The Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers gain the most: a hard ceiling on pain-and-suffering damages, an end to joint liability for those damages, offsets against the patient's own insurance payouts, and an arbitration screen in front of every claim make their losses smaller and far more predictable. Patients would benefit only indirectly, through the argument that lower malpractice premiums and less defensive medicine would slow health cost growth and keep specialists practicing in high-risk fields and underserved areas — a claim the bill asserts in its findings but the text does not guarantee.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the amount providers and their insurers must pay for pain-and-suffering at $250,000 per injury (adjusted for inflation every three years), no matter how many defendants or claims are involved, making malpractice losses predictable.
Ends joint liability for non-economic damages, so each defendant pays only its percentage of fault rather than covering an absent co-defendant's share.

Lets providers pay future economic damages in installments — buying an annuity or funding a trust if the court thinks they might not pay — and bars reopening the judgment even if the patient's condition changes, barring fraud.

Forces malpractice claims arising from Medicare, Medicaid, federal employees' care, or employer health plans into nonbinding arbitration first, and imposes fee penalties on either side that rejects the award and fares worse in court.

States that comply must also adopt quality-assurance measures — cooperating with federal outcomes research, reporting on medical board performance, and requiring disciplined physicians to take continuing education — which the bill's authors argued would reduce negligence itself.

The bill's stated purpose was to lower malpractice insurance and litigation costs that it said were inflating health care prices and driving defensive medicine, and to keep providers in high-risk specialties and underserved areas.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by negligent medical care bear the cost directly: their compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and lost companionship is capped at the same $250,000 whether the injury is moderate or catastrophic; their awards are reduced by payments from their own health or disability insurance; their claims must go through arbitration first; and a claimant who rejects the arbitration award and fails to beat it by at least 10 percent at trial must pay the provider's costs and legal fees. A judgment for periodic payments cannot be reopened if the patient worsens. States also pay: any state that does not enact the required reforms loses a share of federal domestic discretionary funds, and the federal caps would be applied directly to claims involving Medicare, Medicaid, and similar programs in that state anyway.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering applies to a single injury across all defendants and all related claims, so a child with lifelong brain damage from a delivery error recovers the same non-economic amount as a patient with a minor complication — and the judgment cannot be reopened if the injury worsens.

Awards are reduced by payments from the patient's own health insurance, disability coverage, or employer wage continuation, meaning the negligent provider's insurer pays less precisely because the patient was already insured.

Arbitration is mandatory, and a plaintiff who rejects the award and wins less than 10 percent more at trial must pay the defendant's costs and attorney's fees — a penalty that can deter valid claims by people of modest means.

States that decline the reforms face withholding of broad federal domestic discretionary funding, and the federal rules would be imposed on their Medicare and Medicaid claims regardless — a direct override of state control of tort law.
The bill's promised savings for patients are indirect: nothing in the text requires malpractice insurers to lower premiums or providers to lower prices when their liability falls.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem — malpractice premiums and defensive medicine raise health costs, and some doctors avoid high-risk specialties. But its design pays for those savings almost entirely out of the compensation of the most severely injured patients: the cap is identical for moderate and catastrophic harm, the insurance offset shifts costs onto the very people who were insured, and the arbitration fee penalty gives injured patients a wager on their own case. Some savings might have reached patients through lower premiums and prices, but the bill contains no mechanism ensuring that. On balance, this is a liability-protection bill for providers and insurers more than a patient-protection bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of the 102nd Congress, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on October 8, 1992, joined by Sens. Bob Dole, John Chafee, and John Danforth — all Republicans — with about two months left in the 102nd Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day; no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill expired with the committee's record showing only the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients and the lawyers who represent them — malpractice claims remained governed by state law with no federal cap, no insurance offset, and no mandatory arbitration. Providers and malpractice insurers gained nothing from this bill, though many states were adopting their own damage caps at the state level.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients, who kept full state-law rights

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-UT), bill sponsor and senior member of the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. John Chafee and John Danforth
American Medical Association and provider groups
for.what_they_did: Long championed federal malpractice damage caps as the answer to rising premiums and defensive medicine.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Joseph Biden)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 8, 1992 and never reported it out — no markup, vote, or floor scheduling before the Congress ended.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed federal damage caps and mandatory arbitration in medical negligence cases, which it argued would leave catastrophically injured patients undercompensated.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans; the bill received no roll-call vote, and the Democratic-led Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Damage caps, insurance offsets, several-only liability, and unchangeable periodic-payment judgments all directly shrink claim payouts and make losses predictable. The bill's gains for this industry come at the expense of the patients it would otherwise have to compensate.

Providers get capped exposure, mandatory arbitration, and relief from paying for co-defendants' shares of fault. Supporters argued patients would share the gains through lower premiums and less defensive medicine, but nothing in the bill requires savings to be passed on.

Contingent-fee lawyers live off malpractice recoveries; caps, offsets, mandatory arbitration, and fee-shifting penalties shrink both their clients' awards and their own fees. Their interest in this bill runs with that of injured patients.
The periodic-payment provisions let providers satisfy future-damage judgments by purchasing annuities or funding trusts, steering settlement money into annuity products.
